approved: Family Assistance and Child Support Legislation Amendment (Protecting Children) Bill 2018

The majority voted in favour of keeping [part 2 of schedule 1](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;db=LEGISLATION;id=legislation%2Fbills%2Fr5976_third-reps%2F0001;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbills%2Fr5976_third-reps%2F0000%22;rec=0#5eaa6ce3e3cc4a508d30fa29bb1d9a05) unchanged. In parliamentary jargon, they voted for that part to "stand as printed". This vote was put after Labor Senator [Louise Pratt](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/louise_pratt) moved that that part should be opposed, [explaining that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-05-09.4.2) the Labor Party was concerned *"that the retrospective application of amended child support assessments will have negative consequences"*. Read more about [the bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5976) and what it does in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd079).

The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-05-09.11.1) introduced by Senator [Louise Pratt](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/louise_pratt), which means they failed. The amendments related to the new ability of the Child Support Registrar to retrospectively change a child support assessment. Senator Pratt [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-05-09.11.1): > *It is simply not fair for a parent who has received child support in good faith and has spent it on their children to find out that, through no fault of their own, that money must now be repaid. It is simply unsustainable for us to consider having such a big impact on a family's ability to meet the cost of living. This is why we are moving this amendment today to part 2 of schedule 1 of the bill to attempt to deal with this issue ... This amendment permits the Child Support Registrar to change a child support assessment, following the amendment of an income tax assessment, prospectively and retrospectively in limited circumstances. A child support assessment can only be made retrospective if either the amendment was due to fraud or evasion or the registrar is satisfied that changing the administrative assessment retrospectively would not cause the parent unjustified financial hardship, having regard to the financial situation of the other parent.* Read more about the changes made by [the bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5976) in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd079).

Labor supported the No Jab, No Pay component and most child support changes in the bill, but raised concerns that retrospective tax assessment amendments could create unexpected debts for child support recipients who had spent payments in good faith. The party reserved its final position pending further information from the minister.

The member for Dunkley supported the Family Assistance and Child Support Legislation Amendment (Protecting Children) Bill 2017, arguing it would improve child support processes and care arrangements, including terminating agreements when a parent's care falls below 35%, and change immunisation penalties for family tax benefit from an end-of-year supplement reduction to fortnightly withholdings.

The bill amends the child support program to extend interim care dispute periods, ease variation of pre-2008 binding agreements, and allow retrospective tax assessment adjustments, and strengthens No Jab, No Pay by withholding $28 per fortnight from Family Tax Benefit Part A for children not fully immunised. The speaker supported the bill but noted Labor's concerns about retrospective child support changes.

The speaker supported the No Jab, No Pay changes—including the new $28-per-fortnight Family Tax Benefit Part A withholding—but raised concerns about child support amendments that could create unexpected debts for recipients who spent payments in good faith, and noted the bill addresses only three of the 25 recommendations from the 2015 “From conflict to cooperation” inquiry.

The speaker supported most provisions of the Family Assistance and Child Support Legislation Amendment (Protecting Children) Bill 2017, including the "No Jab, No Pay" immunisation policy and extended interim care determination periods, but reserved final position due to concerns that retrospective child support debt adjustments could unfairly burden payees, particularly women, who spent payments in good faith. The speaker noted only three of 25 recommendations from a 2015 child support inquiry had been implemented, and condemned Senator Pauline Hanson for anti-vaccination comments.

The member supported the bill’s extension of interim care periods beyond the current 14–26 weeks, citing a constituent’s case of a parent exploiting child support rules after contravening court orders. He criticised the government for failing to pass the legislation by 1 January 2018, attributing the delay to a cancelled parliamentary sitting week.

The bill links immunisation and health check requirements to family tax benefit Part A, reducing fortnightly payments by around $28 for non-compliant children after a 63-day grace period, and introduces child support reforms including $12.4 million for three priority recommendations, new interim periods for disputed care arrangements, and expanded rules for amended tax assessments and child support agreements.
